did_you_know.text: The word “maḥteret” is related to breaking through or digging into a wall, so it may describe a thief breaking into a house at night. The law distinguishes between an immediate danger and a thief who can be identified without posing a threat to life.

“He shall be sold for his theft” reflects an ancient society in which a person could be sold into labor to cover a debt or compensation. This was not imprisonment, but an economic way to repay the loss.
In Biblical Hebrew, the word “Elohim” can refer both to God and to judges or a court. In this legal context, it can be understood as a judgment before a judicial authority.

Repaying double is not only compensation; it is also a punishment meant to discourage betrayal of trust between neighbors. Responsibility is determined after an investigation and judgment, not by suspicion alone.
A “mohar” was a marriage payment given to the bride’s family in many ancient Near Eastern societies. It was not exactly the same as a dowry, which was property brought by the bride into the marriage.

In the Bible, a “ger” usually means a resident foreigner living within the community, not merely a temporary visitor. Remembering Israel’s own experience in Egypt turns treatment of the outsider into a moral test of memory and empathy.
The word “neshekh” is related to a root meaning “to bite,” probably because excessive interest was seen as an economic bite. The rule especially protects a poor person who is forced to borrow.
An outer garment in the ancient world also served as a sleeping blanket, especially on cold nights. Returning it by sunset therefore protected a basic need, not merely a matter of politeness.
The numbers seven and eight here mark a transition from a period of waiting to dedication to God. Elsewhere in the Bible as well, the eighth day often marks the beginning of a new stage.

The phrase “a people devoted to holiness” teaches that holiness is not limited to worship in a sanctuary; it is also a daily way of life. Even the treatment of meat killed by animals is part of distinguishing what may and may not be eaten.
